cls: Non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA)
quick: 5 mg PO twice daily initial; usual 10-30 mg/day in divided doses; max 60 mg/day
May be taken without regard to meals; take consistently
Use only if clearly needed; beta-blockers can cause fetal bradycardia/hypoglycemia near term
Excreted in milk; use with caution and monitor the infant
No major adjustment usually needed; caution in severe impairment
Clearance reduced; use cautiously and consider lower doses
May enhance blood-pressure lowering/dizziness; limit intake
Blood pressure, heart rate, signs of heart failure/bronchospasm; do not stop abruptly
summary: Pindolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocking agent that possesses intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA, partial agonism), meaning it causes less resting bradycardia and less depression of cardiac output than beta-blockers without ISA. It is FDA-approved (brand Visken) for the management of hypertension, used alone or with other agents such as thiazide diuretics. The usual adult starting dose is 5 mg orally twice daily, titrated to a usual range of 10-30 mg/day in divided doses, up to a maximum of 60 mg/day. Because of its ISA it may be useful when bradycardia is a concern, but like all beta-blockers it should not be stopped abruptly (risk of rebound angina/arrhythmia) and is used cautiously in asthma/COPD, decompensated heart failure, and diabetes.
indications: Management of hypertension, used alone or concomitantly with other antihypertensive agents (notably thiazide-type diuretics)

dosage.d: 5 mg twice daily, alone or added to other antihypertensive therapy
dosage.n: Antihypertensive response usually seen within the first week

dosage.d: If response is inadequate, increase by 10 mg/day at 3- to 4-week intervals; usual maintenance 10-30 mg/day in divided doses

dosage.n: Do not exceed the maximum recommended dose

dosage.d: Use cautiously; consider lower starting doses and slower titration

admin: Take orally as prescribed, usually twice daily; doses can be taken without regard to meals but keep timing consistent
Titrate gradually - allow 3 to 4 weeks between dose increases to assess the antihypertensive response
Do NOT discontinue abruptly; taper over about 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound hypertension, angina, or arrhythmia
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate during initiation and titration
Caution patients about dizziness, especially when standing up or at the start of therapy
moa: Pindolol is a non-selective beta-adrenoreceptor antagonist (blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors) that also has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (partial agonist activity). By blocking catecholamine effects it reduces heart rate, cardiac output, and renin release, lowering blood pressure; its ISA means it produces partial stimulation of the receptors, so it causes less reduction in resting heart rate and cardiac output than agents lacking ISA. It has membrane-stabilizing activity at high doses but no significant effect at therapeutic doses. The precise mechanism of its antihypertensive effect is not fully established.

absolute: Bronchial asthma or severe bronchospastic disease (non-selective blockade can provoke bronchospasm)
Severe bradycardia / sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome without pacemaker)
relative: Diabetes mellitus (may mask hypoglycemia warning signs)
Thyrotoxicosis (may mask signs; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate thyroid storm)
monitor: Signs of worsening heart failure (edema, dyspnea, weight gain)
Respiratory status in patients with bronchospastic disease

preg: Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Beta-blockers taken near term can cause fetal/neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycemia, and respiratory depression; monitor the newborn if used late in pregnancy.
lact: Pindolol is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for adverse effects in the nursing infant (e.g., bradycardia), use with caution and monitor the infant, or decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug.
renal: Renal impairment generally does not require major dose adjustment, but use with caution in severe impairment and monitor for accumulation and excessive beta-blockade.
hepatic: Pindolol undergoes hepatic metabolism, and clearance is reduced in significant hepatic impairment. Use cautiously, consider lower doses and slower titration, and monitor for enhanced effect.

major: Other negative chronotropes/dromotropes (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) - additive bradycardia and AV block
Catecholamine-depleting agents (e.g., reserpine) - additive hypotension and bradycardia
Clonidine - risk of rebound hypertension if clonidine is withdrawn while on a beta-blocker (withdraw beta-blocker first)
moderate: Other antihypertensives and nitrates - additive blood-pressure lowering
NSAIDs - may blunt the antihypertensive effect
Antidiabetic agents (insulin/sulfonylureas) - may mask hypoglycemia symptoms and alter glycemic control
Thioridazine and other CYP2D6 substrates - potential for altered levels
minor: Agents that affect hepatic metabolism may modestly alter pindolol exposure
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to meals.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may enhance hypotensive effects and dizziness; advise moderation.
interactions.diagnostics: Beta-blockers may interfere with glaucoma screening and can blunt the tachycardic response used in some cardiac stress assessments.

serious: Worsening or precipitation of heart failure
Rebound angina, arrhythmia, or hypertension on abrupt withdrawal
rare: Cold extremities / worsening peripheral vascular disease
emergency: Symptomatic severe bradycardia or heart block
Acute decompensated heart failure / pulmonary edema

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate at initiation and during titration
Signs and symptoms of heart failure (edema, dyspnea, weight gain)
Respiratory status in patients with reactive airway disease
Blood glucose in diabetic patients (masked hypoglycemia)
Adherence and avoidance of abrupt discontinuation
counsel: Take this medicine exactly as prescribed and do not stop it suddenly - stopping abruptly can cause chest pain, a fast heartbeat, or a spike in blood pressure
It may make you feel dizzy or tired, especially at first; rise slowly and use care driving until you know how it affects you
Tell your doctor if you have asthma/wheezing, a slow heartbeat, or heart failure symptoms such as swelling, breathlessness, or sudden weight gain
If you have diabetes, this drug can hide some warning signs of low blood sugar (such as a fast heartbeat); monitor your glucose closely
Report fainting, severe shortness of breath, or a very slow pulse, and keep all follow-up appointments to check your blood pressure
pk: Antihypertensive effect generally within the first week of therapy
Plasma peak (Tmax) approximately 1 hour after an oral dose
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light and moisture, in a tight container
pearls: Non-selective beta-blocker WITH intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) - causes less resting bradycardia and less reduction in cardiac output than non-ISA agents
FDA-approved (brand Visken) for HYPERTENSION; start 5 mg twice daily, usual 10-30 mg/day, maximum 60 mg/day
Never stop abruptly - taper to avoid rebound angina, arrhythmia, or hypertension
ISA may make it less ideal where marked heart-rate reduction is desired (e.g., it is generally not preferred for secondary prevention after MI)
Non-selectivity means caution/contraindication in asthma and bronchospastic disease and it can mask hypoglycemia in diabetics
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once. Never stop the medication on your own, as abrupt discontinuation can be dangerous.
overdose: Overdose can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, heart failure, AV block, and bronchospasm. Management is supportive and based on symptoms: atropine for bradycardia, IV fluids/vasopressors for hypotension, glucagon for refractory bradycardia/hypotension, beta-agonists (e.g., isoproterenol) and bronchodilators for bronchospasm, and a temporary pacemaker for high-grade block. Monitor and treat in a setting capable of cardiac support; pindolol is not efficiently removed by dialysis.
